title: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
summary: How CUTLASS builds near-peak GEMMs: a hierarchy of CTA, warp and MMA tiles, CuTe layouts and layout algebra for partitioning, TiledMMA and TiledCopy, and Hopper TMA pipelines with warp specialization.
outcomes: Compute the arithmetic intensity of a GEMM tile and explain why CUTLASS tiles at CTA, warp and instruction level
Evaluate a CuTe layout Shape:Stride at 1-D, 2-D and hierarchical coordinates
Use composition, zipped_divide, local_tile and local_partition to reason about who owns which element
Explain how MMA atoms become TiledMMA and how a TMA pipeline with producer and consumer warps hides latency
Compute stage counts and wave counts, and choose between tile shapes, schedules and split-K for a problem

lessons.title: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles

blocks.md:
A GEMM computes $C = \alpha AB + \beta C$ with $A$ of size $M \times K$, $B$ of size $K \times N$ and $C$ of size $M \times N$. It does $2MNK$ floating point operations (one multiply and one add per term) but touches only $MK + KN + MN$ elements. For $M=N=K=4096$ that is about 137 billion operations on about 50 million elements: in principle each element can be reused thousands of times.

From the roofline course you know the catch: a kernel only gets that reuse if the data actually stays in fast memory between uses. Otherwise it is pinned under the memory-bandwidth roof.

Start with the naive kernel: one thread per output element, each thread walks a row of $A$ and a column of $B$ straight from global memory. Every multiply-add (2 operations) needs one element of $A$ and one of $B$. In FP16 (2 bytes per element) that is 4 bytes per 2 operations, an arithmetic intensity of **0.5 FLOP per byte**. Neighbouring threads load the same values again and again, and nothing is kept on chip on purpose.

blocks.prompt: Suppose a thread block instead copies a $b \times b_K$ slice of $A$ and a $b \times b_K$ slice of $B$ into shared memory and computes a full $b \times b$ block of $C$ from them. How does the arithmetic intensity of that step grow with the tile edge $b$?
blocks.reveal: It grows **linearly** with $b$. The step loads $(b + b)\,b_K$ elements but performs $2\,b \cdot b \cdot b_K$ operations, because every loaded element of $A$ is reused across all $b$ columns of the $C$ tile and every element of $B$ across all $b$ rows. In FP16 the intensity is $2b^2 b_K / (2b\,b_K \cdot 2) = b/2$ FLOP per byte: 32 for $b=64$, 64 for $b=128$. The $b_K$ depth cancels out, so it only sets how much data each step stages.

blocks.caption: Arithmetic intensity of one CTA tile step, counting only the A and B bytes it brings in from global memory. s is bytes per element (2 for FP16).

blocks.title: Tile arithmetic intensity grows with tile size

y.label: FLOP per byte from global memory

scenes.caption: Naive kernel: 0.5 FLOP per byte in FP16, whatever the problem size. It lives deep under the bandwidth roof.
Square FP16 tiles: 64x64 gives 32 FLOP per byte, 128x128 gives 64. Doubling both tile edges doubles the reuse.
A 256x128 tile reaches about 85 FLOP per byte. The curve flattens: widening only one side helps less than growing both.
FP32 inputs (4 bytes) halve every value. Smaller data types make the same tile more compute bound.

blocks.md: Big tiles are not free. A tile has to fit in shared memory, its accumulators have to fit in registers, and a tile that is too big leaves too few tiles to keep every SM busy. CUTLASS answers with a **hierarchy**: the same blocking idea is applied once per level of the memory hierarchy, and each level matches a level of parallelism in the hardware.

scenes.caption: Each CTA (thread block) owns one tile of C and loops over K, copying a slice of A and B from global into shared memory per step.
Inside the CTA, each warp loads its part of the shared tile into registers. Shared memory is read many times, global memory once per step.
Each warp issues a grid of small Tensor Core MMA instructions over its register fragments, accumulating in registers.
After the K loop, the epilogue applies alpha and beta (and any fused elementwise op) and writes the tile out with coalesced stores.

blocks.md: The CUTLASS documentation writes the whole structure as one loop nest. The outer two loops are parallel across CTAs (the grid launch), the `cta_k` loop is the **mainloop** whose iterations are pipeline stages, and the inner loops over warps and MMA instructions are fully unrolled at compile time.

blocks.code:
for (cta_n = 0; cta_n < GemmN; cta_n += CtaTileN)          // parallel: CTAs
  for (cta_m = 0; cta_m < GemmM; cta_m += CtaTileM)
    for (cta_k = 0; cta_k < GemmK; cta_k += CtaTileK)      // mainloop: one stage
      for (warp_n ...; warp_m ...)                          // parallel: warps
        for (warp_k = 0; warp_k < CtaTileK; warp_k += WarpTileK)
          for (mma_k ...; mma_n ...; mma_m ...)             // unrolled MMAs
            mma_instruction(d, a, b, c);                     // Tensor Cores
blocks.caption: Condensed from the loop nest in CUTLASS's Efficient GEMM in CUDA document.

blocks.md: Concretely, for $M=N=K=4096$ with a $128 \times 128$ CTA tile there are $32 \times 32 = 1024$ output tiles, so 1024 CTAs. With $b_K = 64$, each CTA runs $4096 / 64 = 64$ mainloop iterations.

Every level of the hierarchy does the same thing: stage a tile in a faster, smaller memory and reuse it across as many math operations as the capacity of that memory allows. Tile shapes are the main tuning knobs of a CUTLASS GEMM.

Intensity per tile is not the whole story. Two CTAs that share a row of tiles both read the same slice of A, and the L2 cache may serve the second read. CUTLASS's threadblock rasterization (swizzling the CTA launch order) exists to make that L2 reuse more likely.

blocks.question: A kernel uses 128x128 CTA tiles in FP16 and is still memory bound. Which change raises the tile's arithmetic intensity against global memory?
options: Growing the tile to 256x128
Doubling bK from 32 to 64 while keeping 128x128
Launching more threads per CTA with the same tile
Switching the inputs from FP16 to FP32
blocks.explain: Intensity is 2 bM bN / ((bM + bN) s). bK cancels out, thread count does not appear, and FP32 doubles s, halving intensity. 256x128 raises it from 64 to about 85 FLOP per byte, as long as shared memory and registers can hold it.

blocks.question: For M = N = 4096, K = 4096 and a 128x128x64 CTA tile, how many mainloop iterations does each CTA execute?
blocks.explain: The mainloop walks K in steps of bK: 4096 / 64 = 64 k-tiles. 1024 is the number of CTAs (32 x 32 output tiles), not iterations per CTA.

lessons.title: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function

blocks.md: Every level of the hierarchy needs index math: which global address holds element $(m,k)$ of this CTA's tile, which shared memory slot it goes to, which thread holds which accumulator. CUTLASS 2.x wrote that math into many hand-built iterator classes. CUTLASS 3.0 replaced them with one vocabulary type from its core library **CuTe**: the `Layout`.

A CuTe `Layout` is a pair (`Shape`, `Stride`), written `Shape:Stride`. It is a function from coordinates to an integer index. For a coordinate $(i, j)$ the index is the inner product of the coordinate with the stride:

- `(4,2):(1,4)` sends $(i,j)$ to $i + 4j$: a 4x2 column-major matrix.
- `(4,2):(2,1)` sends $(i,j)$ to $2i + j$: the same 4x2 shape, row-major.

The docs avoid the words row- and column-major: *majorness is simply which mode has stride 1*.

blocks.tex: \text{index}(c_0, c_1, \ldots) = \sum_k c_k \, d_k \qquad \text{for Shape } (s_0, s_1, \ldots) \text{ and Stride } (d_0, d_1, \ldots)

scenes.caption: (4,2):(1,4). Moving down a column adds 1, moving right adds 4. Stride 1 is in mode 0, so this is column-major (M-major).
(4,2):(2,1). Same coordinates, different strides: moving right adds 1, so mode 1 is the contiguous one (row-major).
((2,2),2):((4,1),2). Mode 0 is itself a 2x2 shape: rows 0 and 1 are 4 apart, and rows 2 and 3 repeat that pair shifted by 1. Still a 4x2 matrix, but neither row- nor column-major.

blocks.md: That last layout is **hierarchical**: a mode of the shape can itself be a tuple. You still index it with an ordinary 2-D coordinate $(m, n)$, with $m$ from 0 to 3. CuTe first splits $m$ inside the nested shape `(2,2)` in **colexicographic** order (the leftmost sub-coordinate varies fastest), then takes the inner product with the nested stride.

Colexicographic order also gives every layout a 1-D coordinate. For shape `(3,(2,3))` the integer 16 becomes the 2-D coordinate $(1, 5)$ and then the natural coordinate $(1,(1,2))$. With stride `(3,(12,1))` the index is $1 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 12 + 2 \cdot 1 = 17$. This is exactly what `crd2idx` computes, and it is why the docs say *layouts are functions from integers to integers*.

blocks.title: Evaluating (3,(2,3)):(3,(12,1)) at coordinate 16
blocks.code:
# shape (3,(2,3)), stride (3,(12,1))
i = 16
# idx2crd: peel off sizes left to right
c0 = i % 3          # size of mode 0
i = i // 3
j = i % 2           # size of mode (1,0)
k = i // 2          # remaining mode (1,1)
# crd2idx: inner product with the strides
idx = c0*3 + j*12 + k*1
print(idx)

scenes.caption: Start from the 1-D coordinate 16. Any layout accepts a single integer for the whole domain.
Mode 0 has size 3: 16 mod 3 = 1 is the row coordinate, and 16 / 3 = 5 is left for the nested mode.
The nested mode (2,3) splits 5 colexicographically: j = 5 mod 2 = 1, k = 5 / 2 = 2. Natural coordinate (1,(1,2)).
Inner product with stride (3,(12,1)): 3 + 12 + 2 = 17, matching the crd2idx example in the CuTe docs.

blocks.md:
Two more terms you will see everywhere:

- `size(L)` is the size of the domain (the product of the shape). `cosize(L)` is $L(\text{size}-1)+1$, the length of array you need so every index is valid. CuTe sizes shared memory buffers with `cosize`.
- Shapes and strides may mix **static** integers (written `_8`, known at compile time) and dynamic ones. Static layouts let the compiler fold all of this index math into constants.

blocks.caption: The default stride (LayoutLeft) is the exclusive prefix product of the shape, a generalized column-major. The Python CuTe DSL in CUTLASS 4 exposes the same layouts.

blocks.md: A layout is just a function: coordinate in, integer offset out, computed as an inner product with the strides. Everything else in CuTe (tiling, partitioning across threads, MMA operand maps) is built by combining such functions.

A CuTe layout is not limited to row- or column-major, and the index it returns is in elements of whatever it is applied to, not bytes. The same function can index global memory, shared memory, registers, or even map thread ids to coordinates.

blocks.question: What index does the layout (2,(2,2)):(4,(2,1)) give for the 2-D coordinate (1,2)?
blocks.explain: The column coordinate 2 splits in the nested shape (2,2) as (0,1). The natural coordinate is (1,(0,1)), so the index is 1 x 4 + 0 x 2 + 1 x 1 = 5. The CuTe docs print this layout as rows 0 2 1 3 and 4 6 5 7.

blocks.question: Which layout describes a K-major 128x64 tile of A (shape (M,K))?
blocks.explain: K-major means stride 1 in the K mode. (128,64):(64,1) moves by 1 along K and by 64 along M. (128,64):(1,128) is M-major, and stride (1,1) maps different elements to the same index.

lessons.title: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning

blocks.md: A GEMM kernel keeps asking the same two questions: *which tile does this CTA own?* and *which elements of that tile does this thread own?* CuTe answers both with a small algebra on layouts, built from one core operation: **composition**.

Because layouts are functions, they compose: $R = A \circ B$ means $R(c) = A(B(c))$. The surprising fact the CuTe docs highlight is that the result is again a `Layout`, and its shape is compatible with $B$. So $B$ chooses *which* elements and in what order, and $A$ says *where they live*.

scenes.caption: B = (4,3):(3,1) is a row-major 4x3 layout, so walking i down its first mode yields 0, 3, 6, 9.
Feed each B(i) into A = (6,2):(8,2). For example B(1) = 3 is A's coordinate (3,0), so the index is 24.
All 12 values match the single layout R = ((2,2),3):((24,2),8). Composition produced a new layout, not a lookup table.

blocks.md: Tiling is composition plus a **complement** (the layout of the elements a tiler did *not* pick, which is the layout of the repeated tiles). `logical_divide(A, B)` returns two modes: the elements one tile picks, and the layout of all the tiles. The convenience form `zipped_divide` groups them as ((tile modes), (rest modes)), so a tile is selected by indexing the rest mode.

blocks.title: zipped_divide of an 8x12 tensor by a 4x4 tiler

scenes.caption: Each cell shows which tile it lands in. Tiling 8x12 by 4x4 gives a rest mode of shape (2,3): six tiles, numbered colexicographically.
local_tile (inner partition) keeps the tile mode and fixes the rest coordinate. A CTA with coordinate (1,2) gets tile 5, a 4x4 view of the original tensor.
local_partition (outer partition) does the opposite: fix a position inside the tile, keep the rest mode. Thread 0 gets element (0,0) of every tile, 6 elements with stride 4.

blocks.code:
Tensor mA = make_tensor(ptr, make_shape(M, K), dA);              // (M,K)
auto cta_tiler = make_shape(Int<128>{}, Int<128>{}, Int<8>{});  // (BLK_M,BLK_N,BLK_K)
auto cta_coord = make_coord(blockIdx.x, blockIdx.y, _);          // keep all k-tiles
// zipped_divide by (BLK_M,BLK_K), then slice the rest mode with (m, _)
Tensor gA = local_tile(mA, cta_tiler, cta_coord, Step<_1, X,_1>{}); // (BLK_M,BLK_K,k)
// split the CTA tile across 32x8 threads, one element per thread per repeat
Tensor tAgA = local_partition(gA, tA, threadIdx.x);              // (THR_M,THR_K,k)
blocks.caption: From the CuTe sgemm_1 tutorial. The Step projects away the N mode of the tiler, because A has no N mode.

blocks.md: The most general partitioner is a **thread-value (TV) layout**: a layout from (thread id, value id) to coordinates of the tile. Compose the data tensor with it, then slice the thread mode with `threadIdx.x`. The docs' example maps 8 threads x 4 values onto a 4x8 tile with `((2,4),(2,2)):((8,1),(4,16))`.

blocks.title: A TV layout: who owns each element of a 4x8 tile

scenes.caption: Thread id per element for the TV layout ((2,4),(2,2)):((8,1),(4,16)). Each thread owns two pairs of neighbours in its row.
Thread 3 owns 4 values: (1,2), (1,3), (1,6), (1,7). Composition hands it exactly these, in its own value order.
Value id per element. V0 and V1 are adjacent, V2 and V3 are 4 columns later: the value mode encodes the per-thread register order an instruction expects.

blocks.md: Composition reshapes, divide tiles, slicing selects. local_tile picks a CTA's tile, local_partition or a TV layout picks a thread's share, and both are just layout algebra applied to the same tensor.

CuTe's naming convention reads right to left: `tAsA` means partitioning pattern `tA` applied to tensor `sA`. Applying the same pattern to `gA` and `sA` guarantees the copy `copy(tAgA, tAsA)` moves corresponding elements, even though the two layouts differ.

blocks.question: In the CuTe GEMM tutorial, a CTA calls local_tile(mA, tiler, coord) and each thread then calls local_partition(gA, tA, threadIdx.x). What does each call keep?
options: local_tile keeps the tile mode and slices the rest; local_partition slices the tile mode and keeps the rest
Both keep the tile mode
local_tile keeps the rest mode; local_partition keeps the tile mode
Both keep the rest mode
blocks.explain: local_tile (inner partition) indexes the rest mode with the CTA coordinate and keeps one whole tile. local_partition (outer partition) indexes inside the tile with the thread index and keeps the repeats, so a thread gets one element per repeat of the thread tile.

blocks.question: You compose a data tensor A with B and get R = A o B. Which property does the CuTe documentation guarantee?
options: R has the same shape as A
R is always injective
R(i) = A(B(i)) for all i in B's domain, and R accepts B's coordinates
R has the same strides as B
blocks.explain: Composition's post-conditions are compatible(B, R) and R(i) == A(B(i)). B defines the domain, so R takes B's coordinates; A defines where those land.

lessons.title: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy

blocks.md: At the bottom of the hierarchy is one hardware instruction. CuTe wraps each one as an **atom**: an Operation struct that issues the PTX, plus an `MMA_Traits` struct with its value types, its shape $M \times N \times K$, the threads that cooperate (`ThrID`) and TV layouts for A, B and C. Atoms exist at several granularities: one thread (an FMA), a quadpair of 8 threads (Volta), a warp (Ampere) and a 128-thread **warpgroup** (Hopper).

Two atoms worth knowing by their numbers:

- `SM80_16x8x16_F32F16F16F32_TN` (Ampere `mma.sync`): a warp computes a $16 \times 8$ FP32 tile over $K=16$. That is 128 accumulators over 32 threads, so **4 floats per thread**; each thread also supplies 8 halves of A and 4 halves of B.
- `SM90_64x128x16_F16F16F16_SS` (Hopper GMMA, `wgmma`; the MMA atom docs call it `SM90_64x128x16_F16F16F16F16_TN`): a warpgroup computes $64 \times 128$ over $K=16$, so 8192 accumulators over 128 threads, **64 values per thread** (packed as 32 32-bit registers of FP16 pairs). A and B are read straight from shared memory through a descriptor, so every thread sees the whole operand tile.

A **TiledMMA** tiles an atom across more threads and more values. The docs build one from the Volta 8x8x4 quadpair atom: a `(2,2)` layout of atoms uses 4 quadpairs (32 threads) to make a 16x16x4 MMA, and a `Tile<_32,_32,_4>` then repeats it over values to cover 32x32x4. A **TiledCopy** does the same for copy instructions: a thread layout, a value layout and a copy atom such as a 128-bit vector load.

blocks.title: Building a TiledMMA from one atom

scenes.caption: The atom is the hardware truth: one Volta quadpair (8 threads) computes 8x8x4.
A (2,2) layout of atoms assigns 4 quadpairs to the 4 quadrants: 32 threads, 16x16x4.
A 32x32x4 tiler repeats the same threads over more values: each thread now issues several atoms per call.
A thread slices its fragments with partition_A/B/C and calls cute::gemm, which loops over atoms and issues the instruction.

blocks.md:
The simplest tutorial kernel, `sgemm_1`, shows the same partitioning with plain thread layouts on a 128x128x8 CTA tile and 256 threads:

- Copy: a 32x8 thread layout over a 128x8 tile gives each thread a 4x1 piece of A (and of B).
- Math: a 16x16 thread layout over the 128x128 C tile gives each thread 128/16 x 128/16 = **8x8 accumulators**, the classic register-blocked outer product.

blocks.title: Outer partition of an 8x8 C tile across a 4x4 thread layout

scenes.caption: Scaled-down version of sgemm_1's tC: a 4x4 m-major thread layout over an 8x8 tile. Each cell shows its owner thread id.
Thread 5 owns a 2x2 set of accumulators spaced 4 apart: rows 1 and 5, columns 1 and 5. It needs only rows 1 and 5 of A and columns 1 and 5 of B.
Rows of the thread layout share A values: threads 1, 5, 9 and 13 all read A rows 1 and 5. sgemm_1 gets this projection with local_partition(sA, tC, threadIdx.x, Step<_1,X>{}).

blocks.title: The sgemm_1 mainloop, one k-tile at a time

scenes.caption: With bK = 8 and K = 4096 the CTA walks 512 k-tiles. tAgA's last mode is the k-tile index left by local_tile.
Each of the 256 threads copies its own 4x1 slice of A and of B into shared memory.
Wait for all copies and all threads. Only then is the whole 128x8 slice safe to read.
Each thread updates its 8x8 accumulators from a column of 8 A values and a row of 8 B values per k: 64 FMAs per 16 loads.
A second barrier stops the next copy from overwriting data still being read. Copy and math never overlap here: that is what pipelining fixes.

blocks.md: Atoms are hardware facts, TiledMMA and TiledCopy are spatial arrangements of atoms, and partition_A/B/C or partition_S/D turn a tile into per-thread fragments. Swapping the atom (FMA, mma.sync, wgmma) changes the instruction without rewriting the loops.

Shared memory layout matters as much as thread layout. The sgemm_2 tutorial pads its shared memory layouts (stride bM + 1) to avoid bank conflicts, and Hopper TMA can write swizzled layouts for the same reason. A layout that is correct can still be slow.

blocks.question: A TiledMMA uses the SM80 16x8x16 FP32-accumulate atom with a 2x2 layout of atoms (4 warps) and no value repetition. How many FP32 accumulators does each thread hold?
blocks.explain: Each atom is one warp computing 16x8 = 128 accumulators over 32 threads, so 4 per thread. A 2x2 layout of atoms adds more warps, not more values per thread: 128 threads cover 32x16 = 512 accumulators, still 4 each.

blocks.question: Why do GMMA atoms on Hopper give every thread the whole A tile in their A layout instead of splitting it across threads?
options: Because Hopper has no registers for operands
Because wgmma reads A and B from shared memory through a descriptor built on the whole tile
Because CuTe cannot partition across 128 threads
To make every thread load A from global memory
blocks.explain: The docs explain that the GMMA descriptor is built on the full A or B tile in shared memory, so the ALayout maps every thread to the same tile (stride 0 in the thread mode) and CuTe checks that the smem layout is valid for a descriptor.

lessons.title: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization

blocks.md: The `sgemm_1` loop copies, waits, computes, waits. While the copy is in flight the Tensor Cores sit idle, and GEMM kernels cannot hide that latency by running many CTAs, because accumulators take a large share of the register file and keep occupancy low. CUTLASS's answer is **software pipelining**: keep several k-tiles in flight at once in a ring of shared memory buffers called **stages**.

Hopper adds two hardware features that CUTLASS 3.x builds on:

- The **Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA)** copies a whole multidimensional tile between global and shared memory from a single thread. It takes a descriptor (base pointer, dimensions, strides, box size, swizzle) created on the host plus tile coordinates, and does the address math in hardware.
- **Transaction barriers** (`mbarrier` in shared memory): TMA signals the barrier for a stage when its bytes have landed.

scenes.caption: Simplified model: a k-tile load takes 4 units, its MMAs take 2. With one buffer every load waits for the previous MMA: 6 k-tiles take 36 units, Tensor Cores busy 1/3 of the time.
Three stages: three loads start at once, and each stage is refilled as soon as its MMA releases it. The same 6 k-tiles finish at 16 units and the Tensor Cores run back to back from 4 on.

blocks.prompt: In the 3-stage model above, the load for k-tile 3 starts at time 6, not at time 4 when the first loads finish. Why can it not start earlier?
blocks.reveal: Because k-tile 3 reuses **stage 0**, and stage 0 still holds k-tile 0 until the MMA for k-tile 0 finishes at time 6. The consumer must **release** a stage before the producer may **acquire** it again. More stages let loads run further ahead, at the cost of more shared memory.

blocks.md: CUTLASS packages this handshake in pipeline classes such as `PipelineTmaAsync`. Each stage has a *full* barrier and an *empty* barrier, and the roles call four methods: `producer_acquire` (wait until the stage is empty), `producer_commit` (mark it full; a no-op with TMA because TMA updates the barrier itself), `consumer_wait` (wait until full) and `consumer_release` (mark it empty).

blocks.title: Producer and consumer around one stage

scenes.caption: The producer waits on the stage's empty barrier. At the start every stage is empty, so the acquire succeeds at once.
One elected thread issues TMA copies of the A and B k-tiles with the TMA descriptor and tile coordinates, then moves on to the next stage.
Meanwhile the consumer warpgroup blocks on the full barrier. When the expected bytes arrive, TMA completes the transaction and the barrier flips.
The consumer issues wgmma on the shared memory tiles, then releases the stage so the producer can refill it with a later k-tile.
The producer, which had wrapped around the ring, acquires stage s again. Loads and math now overlap continuously.

blocks.md: Splitting the CTA into a **producer** warpgroup (issuing TMA) and **consumer** warpgroups (issuing MMA) is called **warp specialization**. Consumers hold the accumulators in registers while the producer only issues copies. CUTLASS's Hopper kernel schedules include `KernelTmaWarpSpecialized`, `KernelTmaWarpSpecializedCooperative` and `KernelTmaWarpSpecializedPingpong`.

How many stages fit? With `StageCountAuto`, the SM90 collective builder divides the shared memory capacity by the bytes of one stage, assuming one CTA per SM. One stage holds a $b_M \times b_K$ tile of A and a $b_N \times b_K$ tile of B, rounded up to 128 bytes, plus 16 bytes for its two 8-byte barriers. The builder's capacity constant for SM90 is 232448 bytes (227 KiB).

blocks.caption: Carveout is shared memory reserved for the epilogue (StageCountAutoCarveout). Reserving 32768 bytes for it drops the count to 6.

blocks.md: A Hopper CUTLASS mainloop is a ring of shared memory stages: a producer warp keeps TMA loads ahead, consumer warpgroups run wgmma on full stages, and full and empty barriers pass ownership of each stage back and forth.

More stages are not automatically faster. Each stage costs shared memory that a bigger tile or a smem-staged epilogue could use, and once loads are hidden, extra stages add nothing. StageCountAuto simply fills what is left.

blocks.question: A 128x256x64 FP16 tile on SM90 with no epilogue carveout. Using the builder's formula, how many stages fit?
blocks.explain: One stage is (128 + 256) x 64 x 2 = 49152 bytes, plus 16 bytes of barriers: 49168. 232448 / 49168 = 4.7, so 4 stages. The wider tile buys reuse at the price of pipeline depth.

blocks.question: In PipelineTmaAsync, why can producer_commit be a no-op?
options: Because consumers never wait on the full barrier
Because TMA copies are synchronous
Because the TMA unit itself signals the stage's full barrier when the bytes arrive
Because the producer and consumer are the same warp
blocks.explain: The CUTLASS pipeline docs note that commit may be a no-op when producer instructions update the barrier automatically, as TMA does by completing a transaction on the stage's barrier. The consumer still waits on that full barrier.

lessons.title: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs

blocks.md:
CUTLASS 3.x organizes all of this into five layers, from the hardware up:

1. **Atom**: `cute::Mma_Atom`, `cute::Copy_Atom`, one instruction.
2. **Tiled MMA and Copy**: `cute::TiledMma`, `cute::TiledCopy`, spatial arrangements of atoms.
3. **Collective**: `CollectiveMma` (the mainloop over k-tiles, with its pipeline) and the collective epilogue. NVIDIA's blog calls these *temporal micro-kernels*.
4. **Kernel**: `cutlass::gemm::kernel::GemmUniversal`, which composes a mainloop and an epilogue and schedules them over output tiles.
5. **Device**: `GemmUniversalAdapter`, the host-side handle you launch.

blocks.title: CUTLASS 3.x layers and where choices live

nodes.label:
MMA and Copy atoms
wgmma, TMA

scenes.caption: Bottom up: atoms are single instructions; TiledMma and TiledCopy arrange them in space across threads and values.
Collectives arrange work in time: the mainloop pipelines k-tiles with TMA and barriers, the epilogue post-processes the accumulators.
The kernel composes one mainloop and one epilogue and decides which output tile each CTA computes; the device adapter launches it from the host.

blocks.code:
using CollectiveEpilogue = typename cutlass::epilogue::collective::CollectiveBuilder<
    cutlass::arch::Sm90, cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp,
    TileShape, ClusterShape, cutlass::epilogue::collective::EpilogueTileAuto,
    ElementAccumulator, ElementAccumulator,
    ElementC, LayoutC, AlignmentC, ElementC, LayoutC, AlignmentC,
    cutlass::epilogue::collective::EpilogueScheduleAuto>::CollectiveOp;

using CollectiveMainloop = typename cutlass::gemm::collective::CollectiveBuilder<
    cutlass::arch::Sm90, cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp,
    ElementA, LayoutA, AlignmentA, ElementB, LayoutB, AlignmentB,
    ElementAccumulator, TileShape, ClusterShape,
    cutlass::gemm::collective::StageCountAutoCarveout<
        static_cast<int>(sizeof(typename CollectiveEpilogue::SharedStorage))>,
    cutlass::gemm::collective::KernelScheduleAuto>::CollectiveOp;

using GemmKernel = cutlass::gemm::kernel::GemmUniversal<
    Shape<int,int,int>, CollectiveMainloop, CollectiveEpilogue>;
using Gemm = cutlass::gemm::device::GemmUniversalAdapter<GemmKernel>;
blocks.caption: Adapted from CUTLASS example 48 (Hopper warp-specialized GEMM), which uses TileShape 128x128x32 and a 4x2x1 cluster. The epilogue's shared memory is carved out before stages are counted.

blocks.md: The **epilogue** runs after the mainloop. The accumulator-to-thread mapping that is best for the MMA is not a coalesced pattern for global memory, so the classic epilogue exchanges data through shared memory and then stores with wide, contiguous accesses. It is also where elementwise work is fused: alpha and beta scaling, bias, activations, type conversion. CUTLASS 3.x composes such fusions with **Epilogue Visitor Trees** (EVT), so the output is written once instead of being reread by a separate kernel.

Hopper offers two persistent warp-specialized schedules. In **Cooperative**, two consumer warpgroups split one output tile in half along M, which lowers register pressure per warpgroup and allows bigger tiles. In **Ping-Pong**, the two consumer warpgroups work on *different* tiles, so one runs its epilogue while the other keeps the Tensor Cores busy. Both are persistent: CTAs are launched to fill the SMs and fetch tiles from a tile scheduler in a loop.

blocks.title: Cooperative versus Ping-Pong, three output tiles

scenes.caption: Simplified model: a tile needs 8 units of Tensor Core work and 2 units of epilogue. Cooperative: both warpgroups share each tile, so the Tensor Cores idle during every epilogue. 3 tiles end at 30.
Ping-Pong: each warpgroup owns whole tiles and they take turns on the Tensor Cores. WG 1's epilogue hides under WG 2's mainloop, so the last tile finishes at 26.

blocks.md: Tile choice also has to respect the size of the GPU. An H100 SXM5 has 132 SMs. With one CTA per SM, output tiles run in **waves** of 132. For $M=N=4096$ and 128x128 tiles, 1024 tiles need 8 waves and the last one has only 100 tiles: 97% average utilization. For $M=N=1536$, 144 tiles need 2 waves and the second has only 12: about 55%.

blocks.title: Tiles per wave on 132 SMs (128x128 tiles)

scenes.caption: M = N = 4096: 1024 tiles. Seven full waves, then 100 tiles in wave 8, so 32 SMs idle at the end.
M = N = 1536: 144 tiles. One full wave, then 12 tiles while 120 SMs idle. Total work is 144 / 264 slots, about 55%.

blocks.md:
CUTLASS's remedies for problems that do not fill the machine:

- **Split-K** partitions K across CTAs and reduces the partial results (a separate reduction kernel in the classic form), useful when M and N are small but K is large.
- **Stream-K** (`cutlass::gemm::StreamKScheduler`), a work-centric decomposition, gives persistent CTAs equal shares of all the k-iterations, so one tile may be split between CTAs.
- **Predication** handles tiles that overhang the matrix edge, at some cost in the mainloop.

When you want the same ideas in Python, CUTLASS 4 adds the **CuTe DSL**, which exposes the same layouts, tensors, atoms and pipelines with JIT compilation.

Fast CUTLASS kernels come from a few choices: tile shape (reuse versus occupancy and wave fit), stage count (latency hiding versus shared memory), kernel schedule (cooperative or ping-pong) and the epilogue fusion. CuTe layouts make each choice a type parameter instead of a rewrite.

A tile that maximizes arithmetic intensity can still lose: it may leave a tail wave, spill registers, or leave too little shared memory for stages. Measure with the CUTLASS profiler across candidate configurations rather than trusting one formula.

blocks.question: A model has M = 512, N = 512, K = 16384 GEMMs, and a 128x128 tile kernel launches only 16 CTAs on a 132-SM GPU. Which CUTLASS technique targets this case most directly?
options: Ping-Pong schedule
Split-K or Stream-K across the K dimension
More pipeline stages
A larger 256x128 tile
blocks.explain: With only 16 output tiles, most SMs idle no matter how each CTA is pipelined. Splitting K (split-K or stream-K) creates more parallel work and reduces the partial sums. A larger tile makes even fewer CTAs.

blocks.question: What is the main benefit of the Ping-Pong schedule over Cooperative on Hopper?
options: It needs no shared memory for the epilogue
It uses one consumer warpgroup instead of two
It removes the producer warp
One warpgroup's epilogue overlaps the other warpgroup's MMAs, keeping Tensor Cores busy
blocks.explain: CUTLASS's docs describe Ping-Pong as giving each consumer warpgroup a different output tile so the epilogue of one overlaps the math of the other. Cooperative instead splits one tile across both warpgroups, which lowers register pressure.
